rows.text: Keep the tall plants north of shorter vegetables so the screen does not rob them of light.

Protect stored tubers from rodents and inspect them regularly for damage or decay.

Replace ageing crowns gradually with vigorous suckers instead of renewing the whole bed at once.

Inspect winter protection after wet weather and keep crowns out of stagnant damp.

Buy sturdy young plants in spring if you cannot provide warm, bright propagation conditions.
Adjust fruit thinning to the variety and the size you want, rather than using one fixed fruit count.
Sow spare seeds to fill gaps.

Give climbers supports at sowing or planting time.
Soak seed only if halo blight has not been a problem.

Keep roots moist from flowering.

Cut heads when ready, even if still small.

Check stored roots regularly and remove any that begin to rot.

Check for slugs; keep earth out of the heart.
Bring a few stored roots into growth at a time for a succession of winter chicons.
Check dark covers for slugs or rot without leaving the shoots exposed to light.

Handle soft stems gently and support developing growth before it becomes heavy.

Water at the roots and avoid handling fragile stems roughly when picking or training.
Repeat small sowings at roughly three-week intervals rather than producing one large glut.
Blanch only a few plants at once so pale hearts can be eaten at their best.

Harvest a stemmy bulb for what it offers now; an elongated bulb is unlikely to swell later.
Maintain a compost mulch on light or depleted soil to conserve moisture through summer.

Choose spacing for your variety and growing method; larger plants need more room.

Sow two or three small batches from April to June.

After forcing, take no more stalks that season and do not force the same crown the following year.

Chop healthy spent stems for compost; tough pieces may need a second composting cycle.
